metadata.title: Refusal Is One Direction
metadata.subject: What abliteration actually removes — the refusal direction, and what follows from it
metadata.primary_source: Arditi, Obeso, Syed, Paleka, Panickssery, Gurnee, Nanda — “Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction”, arXiv 2406.11717, NeurIPS 2024
metadata.title_note: Commissioned as “Neuron Abliteration to Uncensor an LLM”, with permission to retitle. Both halves of that phrase are technically wrong: the intervention targets a one-dimensional DIRECTION in activation space, not a neuron, and it removes a refusal BEHAVIOUR rather than releasing withheld knowledge. B01 corrects both on screen.
metadata.scope_note: DELIBERATELY NON-OPERATIONAL. The reel explains a published interpretability finding and its safety implications. It contains no code, no layer indices, no hyperparameters, no model or repository names to clone, and no procedure. The conceptual result is in a NeurIPS paper; the recipe for applying it is withheld. The practical guidance in B07 and B09 is defensive — how to evaluate a third-party edited model before running it.
metadata.note: ai-explainer spine, claude-hai channel, Weekly STEM. FRAMEWORK: three questions — WHAT WAS ACTUALLY CHANGED / WHAT DID IT COST / WHO ELSE TOUCHED THE WEIGHTS. Falsifiability beat is B05, the EMNLP 2026 follow-up: refusal maps to geometrically distinct directions, the shared knob is real but the structure behind it is not one-dimensional, and a linear edit flattens it. B07 is scoped exactly to what the security source demonstrated — a controlled poisoning experiment, NOT a hub survey and NOT an abliterated model. See FACTCHECK.md.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — composer, ask lands answered. Speaks the author's name.
beats.narration_text: I'm Uday Sonawane. There is a technique people call abliteration, usually described as removing a neuron to uncensor a model. Both halves of that description are wrong, and the correct version is a more interesting result — one that the authors themselves framed as a warning about safety training.
beats.new_visual_element: Claude composer, the topic question, answered

shot.show: the Claude composer with the topic question and its three-line answer

props.command: claude "what does abliteration actually remove, and what does the paper behind it claim?"
props.segment: Uday Sonawane · Refusal Is One Direction

beats.role_note: premise correction — two errors in the common description, fixed before anything else
beats.narration_text: Two corrections first, because everything after depends on them. It is not a neuron. The thing being removed is a direction — a single axis in the model's activation space, spread across many neurons and many layers, which no individual unit owns. And it does not uncensor anything. Uncensoring implies hidden knowledge being released. What actually changes is a behaviour: the model stops declining. Whatever it knew before, it still knows, and whatever it did not know, it still does not.
beats.new_visual_element: the two corrections, side by side

shot.show: not a neuron but a direction; not knowledge but a behaviour
shot.visual_intent: Two bordered rows, each with a crossed-out phrase on the left in soft ink and the corrected one on the right in terracotta: 'a neuron' becomes 'a direction in activation space', 'unlocks knowledge' becomes 'removes a behaviour'. The crosses sit beside the phrases, never through them.

beats.role_note: PROOF rubric — three questions for any claim that a safety behaviour was removed
beats.narration_text: Three questions for any claim that someone has stripped a safety behaviour out of a model. One: what was actually changed — weights, activations, or just the prompt. Two: what did it cost — because a change that removes a behaviour can take structure with it, and that should be measured rather than asserted. Three: who else touched those weights — because a downloaded edit is somebody else's edit, and you cannot inspect it by using it.
beats.new_visual_element: the three questions, as a numbered structure

shot.show: three numbered cards: WHAT CHANGED / WHAT DID IT COST / WHO ELSE TOUCHED THE WEIGHTS
shot.visual_intent: Three bordered cards land in a row, one per narration step. The third lands in terracotta — it is the question nobody asks and the one with the sharpest consequence.

beats.role_note: the published finding, with the symmetry that makes it a control rather than damage
beats.narration_text: The finding, from a twenty twenty-four paper at NeurIPS. Across thirteen open chat models, up to seventy-two billion parameters, refusal is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace — one direction per model. Erase that direction from the activations and the model stops refusing harmful instructions. Add it and the model starts refusing harmless ones. That second half is the important half: it is what shows you have found a control, not just broken something.
beats.new_visual_element: the finding and its two-way symmetry

shot.show: 13 models / up to 72B / one-dimensional subspace, then erase and add
shot.visual_intent: Top: two stat cards, 13 models and 72B. Beneath, two bordered rows showing the symmetry: 'erase it → stops refusing harmful' in ink, and 'add it → refuses harmless' in terracotta. The citation strip names the paper, authors and venue.

beats.role_note: why this is a safety result — the authors' own conclusion, quoted
beats.narration_text: Now why this matters, and it is not what the forums do with it. A refusal behaviour is the product of an expensive safety training process, and it survives into the deployed model. This paper shows that behaviour sitting on a single axis, removable by editing weights rather than by retraining. The authors' own conclusion is the sentence to remember: their results underscore the brittleness of current safety fine-tuning methods. That is a finding about how shallow alignment is, published by people trying to measure it.
beats.new_visual_element: the authors' conclusion, quoted and attributed

shot.show: the paper's own closing claim about brittleness
shot.visual_intent: A wide bordered quotation panel holds the authors' phrase in the serif face, with the attribution beneath in monospace. To one side, a small diagram: a thick band labelled 'safety fine-tuning' narrowing to a single thin terracotta line labelled 'one direction'.

beats.role_note: the follow-up — the single-direction account is incomplete, and in an interesting way
beats.narration_text: And here is where it gets complicated, which is the part almost nobody repeats. A twenty twenty-six paper at EMNLP argues the single-direction account is incomplete. Different kinds of refusal — different categories of thing a model declines — map to geometrically distinct directions. But steering along any of them produces almost the same trade-off, so there really is a shared one-dimensional knob. Their conclusion is precise: the different directions affect not whether the model refuses, but how. And a linear edit flattens that structure into uniform behaviour.

shot.show: distinct directions, one shared knob, and what a linear edit flattens
shot.visual_intent: Three bordered rows, each one a claim from the follow-up: distinct directions exist; the trade-off is nearly identical; the difference is how, not whether. The third is terracotta. Beneath, one line: a linear intervention collapses the structure into uniform control. Cited.

beats.role_note: what it does NOT do — and the one claim in the paper that carries no number
beats.narration_text: So what it does not do. It adds no capability. It reveals no hidden training data. A model that stops refusing is not a model that learned something — it is the same model with one behaviour removed. The original paper says the method has minimal effect on other capabilities, and that phrase is worth noticing, because the abstract attaches no benchmark number to it. Minimal is a word, not a measurement, and if you are evaluating one of these models that is the first number you should ask for.
beats.new_visual_element: the three things it does not do, then the unquantified claim

shot.show: no new capability / no hidden knowledge / and 'minimal' with no number attached
shot.visual_intent: Two crossed rows in soft ink for the first two, then a bordered terracotta panel isolating the phrase 'minimal effect on other capabilities' with a chip beneath reading 'no benchmark figure in the abstract'. Cited.

beats.role_note: QUESTION 3 — the supply-chain risk, scoped exactly to what the source demonstrated
beats.narration_text: Question three, and this is the practical one. A security note published last week demonstrates what a modified open-weight model can hide. Be precise about what they did: they did not survey model hubs, and they did not abliterate anything. They fine-tuned a seven billion parameter model with poisoned data, as a stand-in for the kind of weight edit a modified release is. The result is the number that matters — the backdoor fired on its trigger phrase up to a hundred percent of the time, while the model scored ninety-nine to a hundred percent on ordinary tasks. It passes your benchmarks. That is the point.
beats.new_visual_element: the experiment, its scope, and the two rates side by side

shot.show: trigger fire rate up to 100% beside clean task accuracy 99-100%
shot.visual_intent: Two bordered stat cards side by side: 'fires on trigger, up to 100%' in terracotta, and 'clean task accuracy, 99-100%' in ink. Above them, a scope strip in monospace stating plainly: a controlled experiment, not a hub survey, and not an abliterated model. Cited.

beats.role_note: the rubric scored, then the two-sided verdict
beats.narration_text: Scored. What changed: a direction in activation space, by editing weights. What it cost: structure that a linear edit cannot see, and a capability claim with no number behind it. Who else touched the weights: whoever published them, and behavioural testing will not tell you. So — be excited that interpretability can locate a trained behaviour this precisely, and take seriously what the authors concluded from it about how thin safety training is. Be sceptical of anything described as an uncensored model you can download, because that is an unverifiable weight edit from a stranger.
beats.new_visual_element: the rubric answered, then the two-sided verdict

shot.show: three rubric rows answered, then BE EXCITED ABOUT / BE SCEPTICAL OF
shot.visual_intent: Three label-and-chip rows score the rubric. Beneath, two lines: BE EXCITED ABOUT in ink, BE SCEPTICAL OF in terracotta.

beats.role_note: scaffolded task — turned toward evaluating a third-party model, not toward performing the edit
beats.narration_text: Your turn. If you are considering any third-party edited model, ask four things before it runs anything: what base it came from, what edit is claimed, whether the weights are signed or hashed, and whether it has shell or network access in your setup. The last one decides how much the first three matter.
